```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
library(SMSD)
# Three decimal places for numbers written into the text.
f3 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3)
value_of <- function(out, term) out$value[out$term == term]
```

## The Research Question

An information systems researcher is studying how strongly time on task
relates to a usability score among users of a new interface. The
parameter of interest is a population correlation coefficient, and the
deliverable is an estimate accurate enough to guide design decisions: a
confidence interval that runs from "trivial" to "strong" is
uninformative, however significant the correlation. Designing the study
for a sufficiently narrow confidence interval is the accuracy in
parameter estimation (AIPE) approach (Maxwell, Kelley, & Rausch, 2008).

Fixed sample size planning for that goal (`DMAR::ss_aipe_r()`) needs a
planning value for the correlation itself, and the required sample size
depends strongly on it. Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2019) develop
a sequential procedure that needs no planning value and does not assume
bivariate normality: data are collected in stages, and a stopping rule
built on an estimate of the sampling variance of the sample correlation
decides when the interval is narrow enough. `seq_aipe_r()` implements
it for the Pearson product moment correlation, Kendall's tau, and
Spearman's rho. The same article extends the idea to the squared
multiple correlation coefficient, under multivariate normality;
`seq_aipe_R2()` implements that and is the subject of the last section.

## The Method

With <em>n</em> pairs, the sampling variance of the sample correlation
<em>r</em> is approximately the asymptotic variance divided by
<em>n</em>. For the Pearson correlation the asymptotic variance (xi
squared in the article) is a function of the joint central moments of
the two variables up to the fourth order (Equation 3 of the article,
from Lee, 1990); for bivariate normal data it reduces to (1 &minus;
&rho;<sup>2</sup>)<sup>2</sup>. The procedure estimates it from sample
moments; the estimate is the row `xi_squared` of the result and is
written `V` below. With `width` for the target full width of the
interval (omega in the article) and `z` for the standard normal
quantile of the confidence level, the procedure has three parts.

* **The pilot sample size** is the larger of 4 and
  `ceiling(2 * z / width)` (Equation 9). `seq_aipe_r_pilot()` returns
  it; its argument `m_0` raises the minimum.
* **The stopping rule** is met at the first <em>n</em>, at or after the
  pilot sample size, with `n >= (4 * z^2 / width^2) * (V + 1 / n)`
  (Equation 10).
* **The confidence interval** is the sample correlation plus and minus
  `z * sqrt(V / n)` (Equation 11). It is symmetric on the correlation
  scale. The article does not transform to Fisher's
  <em>z</em>, and neither does the package, so in a very small sample a
  limit can fall outside the range from &minus;1 to 1. Whenever the rule
  is met the width of the interval is at most `width`.

## Workflow

The researcher targets a 95% confidence interval with a full width of
0.20, and will check the rule after every 10 new users. The two
variables go to `seq_aipe_r()` as `x` and `y`, paired by position. The
data are simulated from a bivariate normal population with a
correlation of 0.5; in a real study each call to `new_users()` is a new
group of users.

```{r workflow-pilot}
set.seed(113)
new_users <- function(k, rho = 0.5) {
  time_on_task <- rnorm(k)
  usability <- rho * time_on_task + sqrt(1 - rho^2) * rnorm(k)
  data.frame(x = time_on_task, y = usability)
}

m <- seq_aipe_r_pilot(width = 0.20, conf_level = 0.95)
m

users <- new_users(m)
out <- seq_aipe_r(users$x, users$y, width = 0.20, conf_level = 0.95)
out
```

The rule is not met at the pilot, so the study goes on: users are added
ten at a time and the rule is checked after each addition, until it is
met (`vignette("step-by-step-sequential-workflow", package = "SMSD")`
writes such a loop out). To show where it leads, the rest of the study
is simulated here in one piece, 280 more users in the order in which
they would have been recruited, and `seq_path()` applies the check at
every stage the study would have reached. A data frame whose columns
are named `x` and `y` supplies both variables.

```{r workflow-path}
users <- rbind(users, new_users(280))
path <- seq_path(seq_aipe_r, users, width = 0.20, conf_level = 0.95,
                 by = 10)
path
```

```{r workflow-plot, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 6.5, fig.alt = "Two panels. Top: the sample correlation with its confidence interval against the number of pairs; the interval narrows as pairs are added, the stopping point is marked, and the stages after it are drawn in gray. Bottom: the number of pairs rising toward the criterion sample size, which falls steeply over the first stages and then varies between about 250 and 340 until the two meet."}
plot(path)
```

```{r workflow-values, include = FALSE}
final <- summary(path)
final_check <- attr(path, "final_check")
covers <- final$lower_limit <= 0.5 && 0.5 <= final$upper_limit
n_known <- 4 * qnorm(0.975)^2 / 0.20^2 * (1 - 0.5^2)^2
v_final <- value_of(final_check, "xi_squared")
```

The rule was first met at `r final$stop_n` pairs, and that is where a
study run as planned stops; the pairs simulated beyond that point are
drawn in gray and are not part of the result. At the stopping point the
estimate is `r f3(final$estimate)` with a 95% confidence interval from
`r f3(final$lower_limit)` to `r f3(final$upper_limit)`, which
`r if (covers) "contains" else "does not contain"` the population value
of 0.5. `seq_report()` writes the result up:

```{r workflow-report}
seq_report(path)
```

One feature of this result deserves a second look. With the population
variance known, a width of 0.20 at a correlation of 0.5 would call for
`4 * qnorm(0.975)^2 / 0.20^2 * (1 - 0.5^2)^2` = `r round(n_known, 1)`,
that is, `r ceiling(n_known)` pairs. This study stopped
`r if (final$stop_n > n_known) "later" else "earlier"`, at
`r final$stop_n`, because at that point its estimate of the asymptotic
variance was `r f3(v_final)` where the population value is (1 &minus;
0.5<sup>2</sup>)<sup>2</sup> = `r (1 - 0.5^2)^2`. The estimate decides
where a study stops, and in samples of this size it is not a precise
one. A study whose estimate happens to be too small stops early, with an
interval that is too narrow, and that is the subject of the next
section.

## How Close the Coverage Is

The width guarantee is exact. The coverage guarantee is asymptotic:
coverage approaches the confidence level as the target width narrows
(Theorem 1 of the article). At the widths studies use it can fall
short, and the article says so. For the population and the width used
above (bivariate normal data, a correlation of 0.5, a width of 0.2),
with one pair added at a time, its Table 2 (p. 498) reports a mean final
sample size of 204 and coverage of 0.90 for the 95% interval; at a
width of 0.1 the coverage is 0.95, with a mean final sample size of
857. Its Appendix D
(p. 514) traces the shortfall to the estimate of the asymptotic
variance, which is built from ratios of sample moments and tends to be
too small when
the sample is small, so that the rule is met early and the interval is
too narrow.

Simulations of `seq_aipe_r()` as shipped show how the shortfall depends
on the design. The figures are for bivariate normal data, a 95% Pearson
interval, the default pilot, and one pair added at a time. They are
quoted from two help pages, named in the last column, which give the
replication counts.

| Population correlation | Target width | Coverage | Help page |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.4 | 0.4 | 0.78 | `?seq_aipe_sensitivity` |
| 0.4 | 0.2 | 0.93 | `?seq_aipe_sensitivity` |
| 0.4 | 0.1 | 0.95 | `?seq_aipe_sensitivity` |
| 0.8 | 0.4 | 0.69 | `?seq_aipe_r` |
| 0.8 | 0.2 | 0.69 | `?seq_aipe_r` |
| 0.9 | 0.1 | 0.45 | `?seq_aipe_sensitivity` |
| 0.9 | 0.025 | 0.90 | `?seq_aipe_sensitivity` |

Two things stand out. A wide target does poorly whatever the
correlation. And a strong correlation does poorly even at a target that
would be narrow for a moderate one, because a strong correlation is
estimated with little sampling error: the rule can be met with few
pairs, and in samples that small the variance estimate is often zero or
negative, and otherwise tends to run low. A zero or
negative estimate is not used: the check reports the rule as not met,
with a note, and sampling continues
(`vignette("seq-aipe-smd", package = "SMSD")` shows such a check). That
removes most immediate stops with an interval a fraction of the
requested width, but not all of them, and it does not make the estimate
on which a study finally stops a good one. A positive estimate below the
article's lower bound of <em>n</em><sup>&minus;3</sup> is still replaced
by the bound, as the article prescribes, and the rule is then met at
once: 58 of 6,000 simulated studies with a correlation of 0.8 ended
that way at a width of 0.4, and 10 of 2,000 at a width of 0.2
(`?seq_aipe_r`).

`seq_aipe_r_sensitivity()` shows what a planned Pearson study should
expect. For a correlation of 0.8 at a width of 0.2:

```{r coverage-sensitivity}
strong <- seq_aipe_r_sensitivity(true_value = 0.8, width = 0.20, G = 100,
                                 seed = 113)
strong
```

```{r coverage-values, include = FALSE}
cov_strong <- value_of(strong, "coverage")
se_strong <- sqrt(cov_strong * (1 - cov_strong) / 100)
```

In this small run the coverage is `r f3(cov_strong)` (Monte Carlo
standard error `r f3(se_strong)`), in line with the 0.69 in the table,
which rests on 2,000 studies. The mean final interval is
`r f3(value_of(strong, "mean_width"))` wide where 0.20 was the target,
and in `r round(value_of(strong, "pct_variance_unusable"))` percent of
the replications the variance estimate was unusable at one check or
more.
<!-- figures from `?seq_aipe_r` -->
<!-- not from a help page: 0.20 -->

What helps is a narrower target, a larger minimum pilot sample, or
both. With `m_0 = 50` the coverage in these simulations was 0.93 for a
correlation of 0.4 and 0.83 for a correlation of 0.8 at a width of 0.2,
and 0.92 and 0.83 at a width of 0.4. Neither remedy is a cure when the
correlation is very strong: for a correlation of 0.9 at a width of 0.1,
a pilot of 100 raised coverage from 0.45 to 0.69. Before relying on an
interval, run `seq_aipe_r_sensitivity()` at the planned width and pilot
for every correlation that is plausible, the strongest included;
`vignette("sensitivity-analysis", package = "SMSD")` explains its
output.
<!-- figures from `?seq_aipe_r` and `?seq_aipe_sensitivity` -->

## Kendall's Tau and Spearman's Rho

The argument `method` selects the coefficient: `"pearson"` (the
default), `"kendall"`, or `"spearman"`. The pilot, the form of the
stopping rule, and the form of the interval are the same (Equations 30
and 54 of the article are the stopping rules); what changes is the
estimate of the asymptotic variance, which for the rank based
coefficients is computed from the ranks (Equations 27 to 29 for
Kendall's tau and 51 to 53 for Spearman's rho). The three coefficients
estimate different population quantities. For the bivariate normal
population simulated above, with a Pearson correlation of 0.5, Kendall's
tau is `2 / pi * asin(0.5)` = `r f3(2 / pi * asin(0.5))` and Spearman's
rho is `6 / pi * asin(0.5 / 2)` = `r f3(6 / pi * asin(0.25))`.

```{r rank}
stopped <- users[seq_len(attr(path, "stop_n")), ]
seq_aipe_r(stopped$x, stopped$y, width = 0.20, method = "kendall")
seq_aipe_r(stopped$x, stopped$y, width = 0.20, method = "spearman")
```

Each coefficient has its own criterion, so a study must choose its
coefficient before sampling begins; the pairs used here are those of
the Pearson study up to its stopping point, reused only to show the
calls.

In simulations of the rank based procedures as shipped (bivariate
normal data, a 95% interval, one pair added at a time), coverage for a
Pearson correlation of 0.4 was 0.94 for both coefficients at a width of
0.2, and 0.91 for Kendall's tau and 0.87 for Spearman's rho at a width
of 0.4. A strong association is the hard case for them as well: with a
Pearson correlation of 0.8 or &minus;0.8, coverage was 0.91 to 0.92 for
Kendall's tau and 0.87 to 0.88 for Spearman's rho at a width of 0.2
(`?seq_aipe_r`). `seq_aipe_r_sensitivity()` studies the Pearson
coefficient only; for the other two, write the loop by hand as the
sensitivity vignette shows.

### Tied Values

The variance estimators for Kendall's tau and Spearman's rho assume
continuous data. With tied values they are too small, so the rule is
met too early and the interval is too narrow. `seq_aipe_r()` warns when
`method` is `"kendall"` or `"spearman"` and either variable has ties.
Here the two variables are cut into five ordered categories, as ratings
would be:

```{r ties}
rating <- function(v) cut(v, c(-Inf, -1, -0.3, 0.3, 1, Inf), labels = FALSE)
tied <- seq_aipe_r(rating(stopped$x), rating(stopped$y), width = 0.20,
                   method = "kendall")
```

The size of the problem was measured for bivariate normal data with a
correlation of 0.5 cut into five categories: at 200 pairs the variance
estimates averaged 78% (Kendall) and 85% (Spearman) of the actual
sampling variance, and 95% intervals at that fixed sample size contained
the population value 91% and 92% of the time (6,000 simulated samples;
`?seq_aipe_r`). For ratings with few categories, treat an interval from
these two methods as somewhat too narrow. The Pearson procedure does not
assume continuous data.

## The Squared Multiple Correlation

How well do several predictors together account for a response? The
population squared multiple correlation coefficient answers that, and
Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2019, pp. 503--507) extend the
sequential procedure to it.
`seq_aipe_R2()` takes the predictors (a matrix or data frame with one
column per predictor) and the response collected so far. Three things
set it apart from `seq_aipe_r()`.

**It assumes multivariate normality.** The article develops this
procedure for multivariate normal data only, because no distribution
free interval for the squared multiple correlation was available (p.
503). The assumption matters: both standard errors come from normal
theory and are too small for heavy tailed data, however large the
sample. In simulations with three predictors, a population value of
0.50, and a target width of 0.10, coverage of the 95% interval was
0.946 for multivariate normal data, 0.902 for a multivariate <em>t</em>
distribution with 10 degrees of freedom, and 0.788 with 5 degrees of
freedom, and a narrower target did not help (`?seq_aipe_R2`).

**There is a choice of interval.** The argument `ci_method` selects the
interval on which the stopping rule is built. `"wald"`, the default, is
the symmetric interval <em>R</em><sup>2</sup> &plusmn; <em>z</em> (2
<em>R</em> (1 &minus; <em>R</em><sup>2</sup>)) / &radic;<em>n</em>,
with the asymptotic variance of Olkin and Finn (1995) (Equation 59 of
the article). `"log_transformed"` is the interval of Bonett and Wright
(2011), formed for the logarithm of 1 &minus; <em>R</em><sup>2</sup> and
transformed back (Equation 58). The Wald interval is the default
because the article concludes from its simulations that the procedure
built on it did better in terms of the sample size required (p. 506),
and in 59 of the 60 conditions of its Tables 11 to 14 its coverage is
also the closer of the two to the confidence level. The log transformed
procedure, as published, has a pilot of only two more observations than
predictors and no correction term in its rule, so it can stop within a
few observations of its pilot. Neither interval is truncated to the
range from 0 to 1. The Wald stopping rule that the package implements
adds 1 / <em>n</em> to both factors of the estimated variance. Equation
63 of the article, as printed, subtracts it in the second factor; that
form does not reproduce the article's own Tables 13 and 14, and
`?seq_aipe_R2` gives the comparison.

**The pilot sample size depends on the number of predictors.**
`seq_aipe_R2_pilot()` therefore takes `p`, the number of predictors.

A survey asks how well autonomy, supervisor support, and workload
together predict job satisfaction. The aim is a 95% confidence interval
for the population squared multiple correlation no wider than 0.25. In
the simulated population the three predictors are independent with unit
variance and the error variance is 1, so the population value is the
sum of the squared coefficients over that sum plus 1.

```{r r2-pilot}
set.seed(113)
coefficients <- c(0.45, 0.40, -0.30)
population_R2 <- sum(coefficients^2) / (sum(coefficients^2) + 1)
population_R2

survey <- function(n) {
  predictors <- cbind(autonomy = rnorm(n), support = rnorm(n),
                      workload = rnorm(n))
  satisfaction <- drop(predictors %*% coefficients) + rnorm(n)
  list(x = predictors, y = satisfaction)
}

m <- seq_aipe_R2_pilot(width = 0.25, p = 3)
m
employees <- survey(m)
out <- seq_aipe_R2(employees$x, employees$y, width = 0.25)
out
```

```{r r2-pilot-values, include = FALSE}
p2 <- population_R2
pilot_r2 <- summary(out)
pilot_misses <- p2 < pilot_r2$lower_limit || p2 > pilot_r2$upper_limit
```

The rule is not met, and the result carries a note. With
`r pilot_r2$current_n` observations and three predictors the sample
value is `r f3(pilot_r2$estimate)` where the population value is
`r f3(p2)`, and the interval at this stage
`r if (pilot_misses) "does not contain" else "contains"` the population
value. Drawing many pilots of this size from the same population shows
how much of that distance belongs to every small sample and how much to
this one. (`withr::with_seed()` keeps these draws out of the random
number stream of the study itself.)

```{r r2-pilot-sampling}
pilot_values <- withr::with_seed(2019, replicate(1000, {
  pilot <- survey(m)
  summary(lm(pilot$y ~ pilot$x))$r.squared
}))
c(mean = mean(pilot_values), sd = sd(pilot_values))
```

```{r r2-pilot-sampling-values, include = FALSE}
pilot_mean <- mean(pilot_values)
pilot_sd <- sd(pilot_values)
pilot_z <- (pilot_r2$estimate - pilot_mean) / pilot_sd
```

A pilot of `r pilot_r2$current_n` from this population has a sample
value of `r f3(pilot_mean)` on average, already
`r f3(pilot_mean - p2)` above the population value, with a standard
deviation of `r f3(pilot_sd)`. The pilot of this study is
`r formatC(abs(pilot_z), format = "f", digits = 1)` standard deviations
`r if (pilot_z > 0) "above" else "below"` that average: mostly chance,
added to a bias that every small sample has. Both intervals are built
around the sample value, so an interval from a sample this small can
lie entirely above the population value. That is what the note warns
about. With <em>p</em> predictors and <em>n</em> observations, the
sample squared multiple correlation overestimates the population value
by roughly `(1 - population_R2) * p / n` (`?seq_aipe_R2`), which is
`r f3((1 - p2) * 3 / pilot_r2$current_n)` here, and the stopping rule
does not correct for it. The note is attached whenever an interval is
reported from fewer than `p * max(20, 2 * p)` observations (60 with
three predictors, 200 with 10, 800 with 20). It does not change the
stopping decision.

To show where the study leads, the remaining employees are simulated in
one piece and `seq_path()` applies the check after every 10. It cannot
work out the pilot sample size for this procedure, because that depends
on the number of predictors, so the start is supplied.

```{r r2-path}
rest <- survey(270)
employees <- list(x = rbind(employees$x, rest$x),
                  y = c(employees$y, rest$y))

path_r2 <- seq_path(seq_aipe_R2, employees, width = 0.25, by = 10,
                    start = seq_aipe_R2_pilot(width = 0.25, p = 3))
path_r2
```

The check at the stopping point is stored with the path, with any notes
it carries, and it is the place to look before an interval is reported:

```{r r2-final}
attr(path_r2, "final_check")
```

```{r r2-final-values, include = FALSE}
final_r2 <- summary(path_r2)
covers_r2 <- final_r2$lower_limit <= p2 && p2 <= final_r2$upper_limit
notes_r2 <- attr(attr(path_r2, "final_check"), "notes")
```

Sampling stopped at `r final_r2$stop_n` employees,
`r if (length(notes_r2) == 0) "past the range in which the note applies and so without it" else "still within the range of the note, which the check carries"`,
with an interval from `r f3(final_r2$lower_limit)` to
`r f3(final_r2$upper_limit)` that
`r if (covers_r2) "contains" else "does not contain"` the population
value.

### Many Predictors and Wide Targets

The coverage guarantee of this procedure is asymptotic as well, and it
can fail badly. The stopping rule takes no account of the number of
predictors beyond the pilot, so with a wide target or many predictors
the rule can be met while the sample is still small relative to the
number of predictors, with an interval that lies above the population
value. Simulations of the procedure as shipped, with the default
interval, multivariate normal data, a population value of 0.50, and a
95% level, gave these coverages (10,000 replications each; a blank
cell is a condition that was not run; `?seq_aipe_R2`):

| Predictors | Target width 0.30 | Target width 0.20 | Target width 0.10 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | 0.900 | | 0.948 |
| 5 | 0.845 | | 0.942 |
| 10 | 0.668 | 0.865 | 0.934 |
| 15 | 0.361 | 0.790 | |
| 20 | 0.071 | | 0.903 |

The article's own simulations cover 2, 5, and 10 predictors at widths
of 0.05 and 0.10. The article offers no remedy for the shortfall, and
the function does not alter the stopping rule to correct for it; it
attaches the note described above. What is in the user's hands is the
target width and the pilot. With the pilot at the threshold of the note,
`m_0 = p * max(20, 2 * p)`, coverage in simulations was between 0.896
and 0.932 for 5, 10, and 20 predictors, population values of 0.30 to
0.90, and widths of 0.20 and 0.30, at the price of a pilot of 800
observations with 20 predictors (`?seq_aipe_R2`).

`seq_aipe_R2_sensitivity()` runs the procedure for a population value,
width, and number of predictors, and is quick enough to run for every
design under consideration. For the survey above, and for the same
target with 10 predictors:

```{r r2-sensitivity}
designs <- lapply(c(3, 10), function(p) {
  seq_aipe_R2_sensitivity(true_value = population_R2, width = 0.25, p = p,
                          G = 500, seed = 113)
})
mean_n <- sapply(designs, function(out) out$value[out$term == "mean_n"])
coverage <- sapply(designs, function(out) out$value[out$term == "coverage"])
data.frame(
  predictors = c(3, 10),
  mean_n = mean_n,
  coverage = coverage,
  se_coverage = sqrt(coverage * (1 - coverage) / 500)
)
```

In these runs the coverage is `r f3(coverage[1])` for the survey as
designed and `r f3(coverage[2])` with 10 predictors; the standard
errors in the last column are those of 500 replications, and a design
that will be reported deserves 10,000. A width of 0.25 is a wide target
for this procedure, and a narrower one does better. In a second set of
runs with five predictors and a population value of 0.50 (10,000
replications at each width), coverage was 0.851 at a width of 0.30,
0.912 at 0.20, 0.936 at 0.10, and 0.949 at 0.05 (`?seq_aipe_R2`). The
figures at 0.30 and 0.10 are not those of the table above, 0.845 and
0.942, because the runs are separate; the differences are of the size
Monte Carlo error produces, each figure having a standard error of
`r f3(sqrt(0.94 * 0.06 / 10000))` to `r f3(sqrt(0.85 * 0.15 / 10000))`.

When a planning value is available, DMAR has a confidence interval that
inverts the exact sampling distribution of the sample squared multiple
correlation and does not rely on an approximate standard error,
`DMAR::ci_R2()`, and a fixed sample size planner built on that
interval, `DMAR::ss_aipe_R2()` (Kelley, 2008).
